speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the practice established by my predecessors I would like to make a brief report on the ministerial meeting of NATO which was held in London this week, and also to give some impressions of my visit to Cyprus.
My purpose in visiting Cyprus was to pay respects on behalf of the Government of Canada and its people to the United Nations force in Cyprus. I went there in particular to visit the men of the Canadian contingent and to thank them for the services which they and their predecessors have rendered to the United Nations peace keeping effort.
I also took the opportunity to have discussions with President Makarios, Vice President Kuchuk and the representative of the United Nations Secretary General Mr. Bernardes. I also saw the commander of the UN force, General Thimayya, in Geneva on my way to [DOT]Cyprus. The acting commander of the force in General Thimayya's absence is Brigadier Bruce Macdonald of Edmonton, who has already gained the respect of the two communities on the Island. I left Cyprus, Mr. Speaker, prouder than ever to be a Canadian.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
No one could have felt otherwise after seeing the efficient and compassionate manner in which the men of the Canadian contingent are carrying out their varied duties, and I am happy to report this to my colleague the Minister of National Defence.
There is no substitute for personal observation. It was an unforgettable experience to fly deep into the Kyrenia hills where a part of the Canadian contingent carries out United Nations control duties in one of the most sensitive and heavily fortified areas on the Island. There I saw a tiny outpost marked by the flag of the United Nations and manned by Canadian soldiers, interposed between
Greek and Turkish strongpoints on nearby opposing hilltops.
Despite the delicacy and the danger of their assignment the Canadian troops, like the other contingents in the force, do not place a narrow limit on their peace keeping task. A young Canadian medical officer spends a good part of each day ministering to the tragic needs of refugees. Cypriot farmers are driven through danger areas on the way to harvest their crops.
I need not emphasize that in the midst of all the destruction, human misery and economic chaos, the United Nations is playing an indispensable role. I do not believe that the relative stability which prevails on that island today would have been possible had it not been for the United Nations force. An important task of the force is to interpose itself between the opposing lines and to patrol the areas of potential conflict so as to prevent the escalation of minor incidents.
In countless local situations the force, often represented by local commanders of very junior rank, has succeeded in negotiating a cease fire and a local settlement. When local negotiation fails the issues must be taken up with the leadership of the two communities by the force commander or the representative of the Secretary General.
At the NATO meeting I underlined the indispensable peace keeping role that the United Nations force is performing in Cyprus. It is important, however, to recognize that the effectiveness of the United Nations force may diminish in proportion to the fading of hopes for movement toward a settlement. We cannot afford to slacken the impetus toward an agreed solution.
In my conversations I naturally maintained the position that as a contributor to the United Nations force Canada would not advocate a particular solution, but I did urge at every opportunity that there should be early negotiations between the parties. I put this view not only to the President and Vice President of Cyprus but to the foreign ministers of Greece and Turkey, with whom I had private talks in London. I was therefore encouraged as I listened to the constructive statements they made in the NATO Council confirming that they had agreed to meet together with
May 14, 1965

Report on NATO and Cyprus a view to normalizing relations between Greece and Turkey and to improving the situation in Cyprus.
The NATO meetings in London provided an opportunity for an important and timely review of current problems. There was frankness and understanding; and despite the differences which admittedly exist in national viewpoints on some questions, I came away encouraged by the degree of basic cohesion and good will among members of the alliance. This meeting was a good example of the growing fact of NATO consultation. I can do no more than all my predecessors have done in reporting on these NATO meetings; that is, to respect the confidential nature of the discussions, which of course embraced vital problems of interest and concern within and beyond the NATO area. NATO now is concerned inevitably with issues of a global character, and Canada, as a founder member of NATO, is profoundly concerned with the future of the transatlantic alliance.
Last December, on Canadian initiative, it was agreed that in view of fundamental changes since 1949 inside and outside the alliance the time had now come for NATO countries to consider the future of their association and the common purposes and objectives which keep the alliance together. Our purpose was to encourage other NATO members to examine the kind of alliance that could continue to provide security for its members yet be sufficiently flexible to cope successfully with changed conditions.
At the recent meeting in London this study was given further impetus, and there is now a possibility that the future of the alliance will be the subject of continuing discussion in the Permanent Council and at the Ministerial Meeting next December in Paris, if this seems appropriate. I use the latter phrase "if this seems appropriate" advisedly, because it would be regrettable if any issue were raised which might cause any measure of serious disunity within the alliance itself.
On my way from Cyprus to London I was very glad to be able to open officially the Canadian Consulate General in Marseilles under Mr. Eugene Bussiere.
In addition to visiting Cyprus and attending the NATO meeting I had the benefit of discussions with the French Foreign Minister, M. Couve de Murville, as well as with the British Foreign Secretary, Mr. Stewart, whom I met for the first time; the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations, Mr. Bot-tomley, and Mr. Anthony Greenwood, the

Colonial Secretary, with whom I discussed Commonwealth Caribbean questions. I profited greatly from these talks which ranged widely over topics of mutual interest. I also held useful talks with a group of Canadian heads of diplomatic missions who had assembled to discuss matters of importance concerning Western Europe.
From these talks I have returned convinced that despite present differences in the western community there is a serious common determination to consider how NATO could adjust to changing circumstances. There can be no doubt about the need for preserving this alliance in the present state of the world.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
It is a
pleasure to welcome the Secretary of State for External Affairs back among us. Had I known when he was coming I would have gone to the airport to meet him. Perhaps because of my lowly status he would find this appropriate, considering the treatment he received on one of his arrivals abroad. However, he is not a man, nor am I, to indulge in anything acrimonious or bitter. It is a pleasure to follow the Minister, but it is also something of a challenge. His style is so fluid and his syntax so varied that I am reminded of the challenge that was faced by King Richard in Ivanhoe, when his mighty sword could not find any resistance in Saladin's pillow.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext: I think the Minister, as all returning Ministers, spoke with optimism and spoke as the good international that he is. I say that in particular in his reference to the Canadian servicemen in strife-torn Cyprus, he spoke for all of us, or surely for almost all of us, when he said that looking upon their record and their performance he was prouder than ever to be a Canadian. So say we all.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
I quite agree with him that the UN is indeed playing an indispensable role in bringing about what he described as the relative stability in Cyprus. I think, however, in this whole matter of UN forces, quite frequently-and I know there are terrific difficulties-the emphasis upon peace keeping seems to pre-empt what might be greater efforts on peace making; and we have heard very little of the role of the UN conciliation officers in such trouble spots as Cyprus.
May 14. 196!

I am glad the Minister took some initiative in this regard in his discussions with the Foreign Ministers of Greece and Turkey. Some newspapermen suggested that the Canadian initiative was not as great as the press releases said, but I am more of a Canadian than a Conservative and I hope it was just as great as all the press releases indicated. Certainly no matter how important and how effective is the quasi-military operation, the move must be made ever stronger toward a settlement, a conciliation, a pacification.
In reference to the NATO Council, we are faced with the constant difficulty which presents itself after any such meeting, which naturally must take place in an area of confidentiality. I think we all agree with the Minister that the NATO alliance requires at this present time a serious reappraisal, not only in the face of its growing weaknesses but in the face of modern realities in the foreign policy of the great countries of the world and the obvious and clear realignments that are taking place before our very eyes. It is difficult to comment on this, because it is difficult to know what went on.
I noted that the Minister spoke very briefly about his visit to France. I do hope that in his high level discussions there after he arrived in the City of Paris he was able to impress upon the responsible Ministers of that country the very sort of attitude which a fortnight ago he expressed in reference to the sovereign personality of this country in the international community. I note that in today's papers we find indications that continue to cause anxiety as to the movement and incursions in the field of international affairs by those who represent the Provinces in this country. The whole field of international relations is sufficiently complex, heaven knows, without its difficulties being exacerbated further by internal differences within any country.
That is all I want to say. I am glad too that the Minister reiterates the role of the UN and our continuing belief that the UN forms a basic cornerstone of our foreign policy. After I have had a chance to read the statement in full I hope that at some future date, when we have that long delayed external affairs debate, I might have an opportunity to discuss it further. Meanwhile we are glad to welcome the Minister home.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us are glad to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs back
Report on NATO and Cyprus in his place. We hope his efforts will attain some measure of success, because we are sure he spent his time overseas in trying to promote peace wherever he could give some assistance in that direction. I was hoping that if we had known when he was coming back the House might have presented him with a copy of John Steinbeck's book "The Wayward Bus". The Minister would probably have appreciated that gift and would have liked to read it during the period of leisure which he will now enjoy after his peregrinations abroad.
I am sure all of us were delighted that he was able to visit the Canadian contingent working with the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus. I am sure too that the House was encouraged by the report he has given of the excellent service which the Canadian peace keeping force is rendering in Cyprus at the present time. This is the kind of role for which Canada is admirably suited, and it seems to me that increasingly all our defence plans and all our contributions to discussions on world affairs ought to be directed more and more to the part which Canada can play in peace keeping operations wherever they are required.
I am sure that all Members are pleased at any contribution which the Secretary of State for External Affairs may have been able to make toward bringing together the Greek and Turkish foreign ministers; because I think all of us are agreed that ultimately a solution in Cyprus must be found, and it can only be found by bringing the two contesting parties together as quickly as possible.
With reference to the meeting of the NATO Ministers, some press reports have suggested that Canada was probably too aggressive in promoting the role of the United Nations. I think it would be the sense of the House if I said to the Minister that I doubt whether any Canadian representative at NATO can be too aggressive about promoting the role of the United Nations. I think the voice of Canada raised at the conference on behalf of a greater role for the United Nations will receive the widespread support not only of the people of Canada but of a great many people throughout the western world.
I think all of us are glad to learn that there is going to be a continuing study as to the changes which will be required in the North Atlantic Treaty alliance. This alliance, which came into being in 1948 to meet a given situation, will have to be altered in view of the fact that the situation has
May 14, 1965

Report on NATO and Cyprus substantially changed. One of the reasons there has been considerable dissension within NATO itself is that NATO has not changed with the changed circumstances to a sufficient extent. Therefore if there is to be a study of the changed role of NATO this could result in NATO becoming an effective instrument for world peace. My own feeling is that increasingly the functions of NATO must be transferred to the United Nations, and that the day must come when NATO will be an instrument of the United Nations rather than merely a local security alliance.
On this point I should like to suggest that if NATO is studying what changes are necessary, it is not too soon for the External Affairs Committee of the House to examine this question in order that any recommendations going from the Canadian Government to NATO conferences will have the wholehearted support of all sections of the House. In a few years we shall have to decide whether Canada is going to stay in NATO, and that decision will be dependant upon what NATO's role is going to be in the future, what its function is going to be, what its objectives and purposes are. I think the External Affairs Committee should begin very soon a study of NATO's future role and its future capacity.
I hope the Government will decide to make greater use of the External Affairs Committee. There are a great many points on which Members in all parts of the House are agreed, particularly on the role which the United Nations could play in world affairs. To the extent we can work out a common foreign policy that is supported by all parties in the House, Canada's voice will be strengthened when Government representatives go to sit in the councils of the nations. I hope the External Affairs Committee will be used increasingly to work out a common policy at least on those points on which there is general agreement.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are all in agreement with the welcome that has been accorded to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is also Acting Prime Minister this morning. If we had known of his arrival I am sure that not only would the hon. Member for Queens have been present to meet him, but quite a few others would have been there as well.
We followed the reports of his visits to Cyprus, Marseilles, Paris and London, and not only do we agree with his statement that he

was proud to be a Canadian but if we could set aside our partisan robes for a few minutes I think we would also say that we were proud of Canada's Foreign Minister. In fact I am sure that if some of us would be true to our own feelings for a moment we would agree that we were indignant when we learned that on his arrival at Orly airport in Paris he was not given the full red carpet treatment that Canada and her External Affairs Minister fully deserve.
This leads me to observe that the Minister said very little about his discussions with his opposite number in France. I am sure that in the light of his particular role at this time and in the light of the policies that France is obviously following, Canada must not only take the initiative but must use every ounce of her good will and her status among the nations to strengthen the amiable and agreeable situation that should exist between France and her allies. I am sure the Minister agrees that he and Canada have a very important role in this regard in addition to our role in NATO and our role in the United Nations, having particular reference to peace keeping operations.
In my view the statement the Minister has made with regard to Canada being one of the founding nations of NATO is true in that we should be much concerned about NATO's common purposes and objectives and the role of this organization in coping successfully with the changing conditions we now face which are so vastly different from conditions when NATO first came into being.
Last night we heard a report of the accusation of some member countries of NATO that the Canadian delegation was perhaps too ambitious in that its initiative was too strong for their liking, but I think we should not be too much concerned about that type of criticism. Certainly it is not good enough to stand on the status quo and think NATO can survive just because it happens to have done a good job in the past or because the presence of a peace keeping force in Cyprus has brought about a comparatively peaceful situation. Unless those who are the intentions behind the Cyprus problem, unless those who are members of NATO and among the leading member nations of the United Nations as well push forward in an aggressive and constructive way to strengthen the role of these organizations in the changing scene in the world today, we are going to fail to achieve our objectives and our over-all purpose.
Again we say it is good to have the Secretary of State for External Affairs back in our
May 14, 1965

midst. We are grateful for the work that has been done. It serves to challenge us to face the tremendous needs of the future in all the areas which his report covered.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON CYPRUS VISIT AND NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are glad to join with the other members of this house in welcoming back the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), upon his return to Canada from his long trip overseas.
The minister is certainly one of the most genial members of the house and I think it is always a happy occasion for all to see him back among us.
However, we are sorry about the reception he got in Paris. But I know the minister will understand that the French government was keeping the red carpet treatment, the high officials and what have you, for the next Quebec delegation which is to leave at the beginning of the week to negotiate new agreements with the French government.
In my opinion this is symbolical, because France was always a country whose culture illuminated the world, and with the Quebec government about to negotiate new agreements with that country respecting cultural affairs, it is normal that this official reception, this red carpet treatment be reserved to the Quebec government and its negotiators.
However, Mr. Speaker, we would have been happy if our Secretary of State for External Affairs had also been given such a reception, with a "Turkish rug", perhaps in view of the fact that he travelled close to Turkey before he came back to Canada.
Concerning the minister's visit to Cyprus, we would point out that a year and a half ago he asked parliament for authorization to send Canadian troops to that country so they could act as mediators and bring the necessary help to ensure an agreement and peace in that island which was threatened with a civil war as well as a war between Turkey and Greece.
At that time we were told that the operations would last six months but when that period was over two successive delays of six months were asked.
Since then Canada has been footing the bill for all that. Under the circumstances I think the minister should do his best to convince the other countries concerned to make an effort to come to an agreement as soon as possible so that Cyprus can continue to attend to her business by herself and that other countries do not have to spend millions of dollars to restore peace in the island.

I feel that the countries which have a military force in Cyprus must come up with a pacific solution, since they have now been between the two groups long enough to know what kind of an agreement could be negotiated and respected.
With regard to NATO, we did not get much in formation.
We feel, however, that the minister should strive to give a new direction to the work and goals of NATO and, in my opinion, one of the aims of NATO should be to provide assistance to under-developed countries. Such assistance should be provided in the form of food, technical assistance, agricultural products and farm machinery.
This would be the best way in which NATO could contribute to world peace.

I am pleased this morning to be able to report that Mr. Jean Beetz, LL.L., M.A., of Montreal has accepted the invitation to serve as a member of this important commission.

Mr. Beetz, a professor in the Montreal faculty of law, is a well-known expert in constitutional law.
Like the two other members of the commission, Professor Beetz is a young man of high repute.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that Professor Beetz will bring vigour and insight to the

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Acting Prime Minister. I realize, of course, that he has been away and probably out of touch with events here in Canada; nevertheless in his role as Minister of External Affairs I am sure that when he visited Paris the Government of France would have acquainted him with this matter and he may have an answer. My question is based on newspaper stories appearing this morning to the effect that the Quebec cultural minister, Mr. Pierre La-porte, is negotiating a second distinct agreement between the Government of France and the Province of Quebec. There is a conflicting statement by officials in Ottawa who say there is no question of a second agreement. Can the Acting Prime Minister enlighten the House as to the correct situation?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: QUEBEC-FURTHER AGREEMENT WITH FRANCE ON CULTURAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for giving me some notice of this question. I can assure the hon. Member that I was aware of the matter. When I was in Paris last week the matter of cultural affairs was discussed by me with members of the Government of France. In fact I may say that the head of the cultural affairs department of the Quai d'Orsay, M. Basdevant, will be coming to Ottawa on May 25 to discuss this general subject of cultural affairs.
The House will perhaps recall that I previously indicated that when I saw the French Foreign Minister last December it was agreed between us that we would execute what is called in French an accord cadre, a general agreement, in this whole area. It would provide a foundation for separate ententes by any of the Provincial jurisdictions. Some of the Provinces other than Quebec may be very anxious to share in some of the cultural exchanges which the Government of France undertakes with many countries in the world. Hon. Members are also aware that the general question of making agreements affecting matters that fall within the scope and legislative competence of the Provinces, such as educational and cultural matters, were discussed by the Prime Minister and Premier Lesage last week end.

Hon. Members will appreciate that in view of these discussions with the Quebec authorities and the anticipated talks with French representatives, I feel that I would not want to go any further. I have, however, just been informed that Mr. Laporte has made a statement in the Quebec Legislature this morning, and I am advised that it would be proper for me to make reference to one or two things he has said, if I can find the document.

The trip of the minister for cultural affairs to Paris has only been decided a few days ago. It has been deemed necessary to carry on negotiations already under way with France and to prepare the way for other negotiations. It should be noted that the timing of this trip will allow the minister for cultural affairs to attend the premiere of a play put on by the "Theatre du Rideau Vert" on May 19.
When I was in Paris, I was too busy to go to the theatre.
The deputy minister for cultural affairs, Mr. Fregault. has, at my request, sent a letter to the deputy minister for federal-provincial affairs, Mr. Morin, covering in general terms the subjects to be studied in Paris. That letter, in my opinion, should be added to the file of negotiations underway between the government of Canada and the province of Quebec.
Certain people seem to have been anxious to interpret my attitude as a quarrel with Ottawa, rather than tc see it for what it is: the hope to reach an understanding on this most ticklish question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was asked at a press conference if I had any views about the interposition of a force under the Organization of American States, and I did say that while as a strong United Nations man I prefer to see operations of this kind come under the United Nations, it could be desirable in the circumstances that there should be an intervention made by some collective security organization. Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs relating to the NATO conference. Did the Minister at that conference advance the proposal of the Canadian government, announced over two years ago, to negotiate out of its nuclear role within the NATO alliance and within NORAD?

May 14. 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NATO-DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING NUCLEAR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I recognize my hon. friend's persistent and proper interest in this question. The conference was a meeting of foreign ministers. Mr. Speaker, I would like at this stage to refer to the question asked by the hon. Member for Port Arthur on April 29 concerning radio station CHFI in Toronto. I have received the following information from the Board of Broadcast Governors.
The application before the Board on March 24 dealt with the transfer of shares in 1540 Limited, Toronto. The approval of the Board in such matters is required by section 118 of the radio regulations. In these cases the Board cannot choose between contending applicants; it can only deal with such applicants as have already entered into a conditional contract of purchase and sale of company shares with the original owner of those shares.
In this instance the Board was satisfied with the financial resources of the applicants and with the programming policy the applicants were willing to follow. Although representations were received by the Board objecting to the transfer, there was no evidence in these representations to change the Board's views. The answer is as follows. Walsh Advertising Company Limited, Toronto, made an

Mar 14, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry assignment in bankruptcy on April 2, 1965, and the first meeting of the creditors had been called for April 20, 1965. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition inquired as to whether one Georges Lemay, a most wanted man, had entered Canada on April 23 and, after a short stay, had returned to the United States. I undertook to make a statement on the matter today.
In the course of his remarks the right hon. gentleman referred to certain articles in the press. I said that I had read one of the articles, and I have since had the opportunity of reading another one. I have made an investigation, and I am informed that on January 23, 1962 the Montreal police put out a "Wanted" circular for Lemay in connection with the robbery of the Bank of Nova Scotia, which had occurred on July 1, 1961. On January 31,1962, the R.C.M.P. were brought into the picture and I am informed that they distributed information on a routine basis to police forces in Canada, in different parts of the United States and elsewhere. Such an alert by the police does not, so far as I have been able to ascertain, include the Canadian immigration service. Our service, the immigration service, is concerned with aliens coming into Canada, not with people leaving Canada.
In this connection I might say that the first newspaper article referred to by the right hon. gentleman in his statement yesterday was a press item which alleged that the said Lemay had been in Vancouver in 1963. Now, Mr. Speaker, he may or may not have been in Vancouver, but even if he were this is not a matter which would involve my Department. Lemay is a Canadian. So far as I know-and I do not think I would be here if the circumstances were otherwise-going to Vancouver does not involve going through immigration.
With regard to the other suggestion, Mr. Speaker, that the said Lemay had entered Canada on April 23 of this year, and after a short stay, had returned to the United States, may I say that after careful consideration I do not consider it proper to comment at this time on this aspect. One of the said newspaper articles alleges that the U.S. immigration service has charged Lemay with illegal entry into the United States at Rouses Point, some 70 miles from Montreal. The article alleges that Lemay represented himself to be a United

May 14, 1965
Inquiries of the Ministry States citizen, and that he produced a United States driving licence in the name of Rene Roy. Rouses Point is a U.S. border point. There is no Canadian port by that name. I might say there are several ports on the Canadian side that are served by a series of roads that come out from Rouses Point, but the immigration duties with regard to cars at these points are conducted by customs officers, not by immigration officers.
In any event, in the same article referred to by the right hon. gentleman a woman who claimed to be Mrs. Lemay is said to have denied that her husband did return to the United States on that occasion. She claims, according to the article, that he never left the United States and so could not have returned to the United States. Therefore this matter, being the subject of a charge in the United States courts, is sub judice, and I do not think I should comment on the truth or otherwise of the newspaper statements. However, Mr. Speaker, I think it is fitting for me to say to Members who are interested that in this particular incident, that, as a result of the effective co-operation of the authorities, including the police of Montreal, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and police officials in the United States, a much wanted man has been arrested and presumably he will be returned to Canada in due course under extradition proceedings.

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-101, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Some of my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, have been asking me to make this interesting since it has been a very dull morning. I am afraid I cannot come through with anything exciting on the Bank of Canada Act. I spoke briefly last night and I only intend to take a little time this morning.
There are one or two aspects of the Bill with which I did not deal last night to which I should like to refer this morning. Before doing so I should like to repair an omission of last night. I neglected to associate myself with the Minister's remarks relating to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. I have been very much impressed when I have been in other countries, having usually arranged to meet the Minister of Finance or the Governor of the Central Bank, sometimes both, when invariably Mr. Rasminsky's name has come up. He has been referred to in terms of the highest admiration. I think we can consider ourselves very fortunate to have a man who is acknowledged to be one of the world's experts in this difficult field as the Governor of our Central Bank.
May 14, 1965

The other important section of the Bill to which I did not refer last night is the one which alters the secondary reserve regulations of the Bank of Canada, or rather gives statutory authority to the secondary reserves that were the result of a voluntary agreement between the Central Bank and the chartered banks up until this time. It seems to me this is a wise move. It will give the Government a bit more flexibility in the use of monetary policy for carrying out their general economic purposes than would have been the case if we continued with this so-called voluntary arrangement.
There is, however, one aspect of this whole question that I think might well be stressed today, and that is the use of monetary policy as a means of expansion and development of the economy. I should like to throw out a suggestion which is based, shall I say, on the views of a great many economists, some of whom I have consulted personally and some of whom I have consulted via the written word. This has to do with the fixed exchange rate and the possible advantage that might accrue from reverting to a floating exchange rate such as we had up until a year or two ago.
I am well aware of our agreement under the International Monetary Fund agreement, and the International Monetary Fund might gnash their teeth a bit. However, it does seem the Minister might well explore this possibility, because I think there can be no doubt that the existence of a fixed exchange rate does, to a great extent, limit the Government's power to use monetary policy in pursuit of domestic government policies. The weapon has to be ready at all times to be used to support Canadian currency against any downward pressures.
I know there are contrary opinions with regard to this, but I hope at some point the Minister might express his views on this subject, either in the House or before the Banking and Commerce Committee. I think the article which appears in this morning's Globe and Mail quoting Dr. Bora Laskin, Professor of Constitutional Law at the University of Toronto, might have some bearing on this question. Professor Laskin charges Federal Legislatures with having allowed a steady attrition of Federal powers since the Second World War, and the lack of boldness for experiments necessary to expand them. He is quoted as saying this:
It seems to me a truism that power contracts by the failure to use it.
Bank of Canada Act
There are problems of national importance which can only be solved by the Federal Government, but it often is reluctant to face the struggle involved.
He suggests that part of the reason for this reluctance can be traced to the reaction against Federal regulation following the end of the Second World War. However, there is another field in which it seems to me this initiative might be taken, and that is the more positive use of the government's fiscal and monetary powers with regard to overcoming the problem of the so-called designated areas. It has seemed to me that the Government has been altogether too timid, too careful, too cautious, and is hoping to achieve the purpose it has in mind with rather inadequate weapons in the way of carrots in the form of tax exemptions, depreciation allowances and so on, and not being prepared to take any definite economic steps itself by the use of its fiscal and monetary powers. I hope the Minister will consider this and let us know at some time if the Government has taken under consideration the possible advantages of negotiating with the I.M.F. for a return to a floating exchange rate such as prevailed up until a few years ago.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-101, to amend the Bank of Canada Act, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) introduced last night shows that the evolution of the monetary system has become irreversible.
We cannot really say that this bill offers any stunning reforms. Is it the minister's modesty that held him back, or is it the power of the Canadian bankers' association upon the party's electoral funds that restrained him from bringing in some major amendments that would have allowed the Canadian economy to progress at the same rate as the population growth? I leave it to my colleagues to answer the question.
We know that the Minister of Finance is a man who wants to repatriate the Canadian economy, but I see no proposed amendment to the Bank of Canada Act which could favour such a repatriation. The Bank of Canada could play a more important part by freeing capital in the private sector and by directing it toward industrial, commercial and agricultural investments.
In his 1964 annual report, the governor of the Bank of Canada mentioned that 14.6 per cent of the debt of Canada, or $3,239

May 14, 1965
Bank of Canada Act
million was held by the Bank of Canada, that chartered banks held 15.9 per cent or $3,691 million of that debt, that foreigners held 8.9 per cent of Canada bonds and, finally, that 60.6 per cent of Canadians had $12 billion in Canada bonds.
The amount of securities kept by chartered banks is too large.
As regards the proportion of 60 per cent held by Canadians, that does not mean individuals, because in fact, the amount of Canada bonds that Canadians, as individuals, keep as investments, is under 10 per cent.
Therefore, the part played by the Bank of Canada must increase tremendously before it takes over most securities issued or guaranteed by the Canadian government.
Of course, I am very happy to note that this measure will restore the supreme authority of the government in monetary policy matters and that it incorporates the bill that I am introducing for the third time in this house and which bears this year No. C-9, in order to remove all misleading words on our bank notes. Here is what the minister said on that matter as can be seen on page 1282 of yesterday's Hansard:
A related amendment Is proposed in respect of notes of the Bank of Canada to remove the description "payable to bearer on demand". Since these notes are themselves legal tender and have never in fact been convertible into gold, the present wording is unnecessary and in some quarters liable to misinterpretation.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a statement which I consider as very interesting.
The legislation now before us also clearly recognizes the inconvertibility of our currency. The old legislation could easily mislead a layman in that matter. As early as 1962, I made every effort to destroy that legend of a gold reserve which, according to many people, guaranteed our currency In view of the fact that from now on it will be specifically recognized that our currency has not been convertible into gold since 1940, I hope that the house will easily pass Bill No. C-25 which I introduce again this year in order to promote our international trade in goods and services by enabling the Bank of Canada to keep in its foreign exchange reserves non-convertible currencies like ours, up to a maximum $500 million.
Finally, the most important amendment to the Bank of Canada Act that the bill should have made, namely that concerning chartered banks' reserves, is but an illusion. Such a measure will, in fact, give more power to the commercial banks. The regalities as to the
[Mr. Cote (Chicoutimi) .1
issuing of new bank money will still be, almost exclusively, the prerogative of the chartered or commercial banks. When will it be realized that if the government is to be the sovereign authority as regards monetary policies, it should not surrender the privilege of issuing new credit to private banking institutions? Such a privilege should be the prerogative of the Bank of Canada, under the aegis of a national credit council.
Even if the minister states that the proposals changing the reserves of the chartered banks will reinforce the Bank of Canada's monetary policy, I disagree with him.
Some people think that cash reserves consist of dollar bills and coins; actually, such reserves only mean any deposit of a chartered bank with the Bank of Canada. The commercial banks' power to create money will seem slightly limited but, in practice, that power will be unlimited if you consider the fact that to keep a constant cash reserve as required, banks only have to deposit cheques issued by the government of Canada, and you can imagine how many cheques the federal government issues every day.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the Minister of Finance that he has missed a wonderful opportunity to go down in history as one of the world's greatest financial geniuses. I have admiration for the minister, but it is not too late, since he has the required authority to give the world a stimulating example of greatness for our country.
Last night, after the sitting, I read in La Presse a statement by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) who exclaimed: Canadians fill up jails twice as fast as cradles.
What is the basic reason for that situation? Is it that the present financial system, under which the nation, governments and private citizens are always getting further into debt, makes it impossible for our young people to look to a better future. That system does not enable them to develop normally, according to the talents given them by Providence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out that it is one o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: Is it the wish of the House that I call it one o'clock?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Agreed.
At one o'clock the House took recess.
May 14, 1965
The House resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to have a few minutes to express my views on the government measure introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to amend the Bank of Canada Act.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people have the right to expect much more than what the minister is proposing. While the Canadian citizen is becoming more and more concerned with the idea of monetary reform, the minister is asking us to delete just a few words from the Bank of Canada notes and, even if those words are inaccurate, that will not increase the value of the bank notes. As monetary reforms go, that is not much.
One thing that is more welcome is where the government wants to take up again its responsibility as regards the monetary policy and its implementation. But here again, it may be that the governor of the Bank of Canada will have to be replaced, if the government wants to apply a truly Canadian policy that could benefit the whole population; the minister said it last night, as recorded in the official report of the debates, on page 1280, second to last line of the right-hand column:
If the government of the day ever issued a directive to the governor to execute a monetary policy which he felt was contrary to the public interest it can be presumed he would resign rather than accept such a responsibility.
In that case, it would be the opinion of the governor which would prevail. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I fear that the Minister of Finance-whether it be the present minister or another one-might be reluctant when the time comes to apply certain economic measures; and the Canadian economic policy is, after all, the responsibility of a single man.
There is another point of great concern to me: chartered banks will be granted greater powers to create credit by being able to reduce their reserve from 8 to 7 per cent. I maintain that this power to create credit should be restricted to the Bank of Canada, at the service of the Canadian government.
The obsolete financial system forced upon us by the old-time parties has resulted in a huge debt of $26 billion for a population of under 20 million, and then we have to pay $1,100 million every year in interest to the controllers of credit. Now, the minister intends to give them even more power so that
Bank of Canada Act
they might extend their control further. Mr. Speaker, this power should be given back to the Bank of Canada, on behalf of the government, which is responsible for the welfare of every citizen of the country.
During the discussion in committee we shall have the opportunity to look carefully into every section of this bill and to move whatever amendments we feel are required. For the time being, so far as I am concerned, I do not intend to make other remarks. I shall have the opportunity to come back to this in due course.

There is no doubt that monetary policy is an integral part of any Government's economic policy as a whole. Monetary policy, fiscal policy and debt policy are interdependent and must be operated in a fully integrated fashion if they are to function effectively. So the part of this bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act which interests me most and about which I should like to say a few words today is that relating to the proposed new section 14 which replaces the old section and which the explanatory footnote tells us "defines the relationship between the Government and the Bank with regard to monetary policy". This is particularly important because of the close relationship there is between fiscal policy, which is clearly within the jurisdiction of the Government of the day, and monetary policy.
There are two elements in this newly defined relationship. One might call the first a consultative one. The Minister and the Governor are now required to consult on monetary policy and its relation to general economic policy. The second element provides a procedure whereby the Government may issue a directive to the Bank of Canada regarding the monetary policy it is to follow.
The first of these elements, the consultative one, simply spells out what ordinarily takes place. Indeed, for many years it was a convention that there should be this kind of consultation, although I suspect the consultation which did go on took place between the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Governor of the bank, rather than between the Minister of Finance and the Governor. Nevertheless there was for many years a close relationship established by convention to deal with monetary policy, and its relation to other aspects of Government policy. Unfortunately, this convention was flouted by the second Governor of the Bank of Canada, or that seems to have been the case, and what this section is

May 14. 1965
Bank of Canada Act
doing is to restore it, explicitly stating that such consultation on monetary policy should take place. I think it is a good idea that it should be set out in writing as it is.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The second part o f the new section 14, requiring the Government to issue a directive should it feel that the monetary policy being fallowed by the Bank is not in keeping with over-all Government policy, is not a novelty except in this country. Most of the bank acts in most countries with a system comparable to our own have had such a government directive section in them for many years. I am thinking of the acts in the United Kingdom, Australia, Holland, and so on. The purpose, as the Minister of Finance said last evening, as reported at page 1280 of Hansard, is to ensure that "the Government can never shirk its ultimate responsibility for the monetary policy which is followed any more than it can for any field of national policy".
The Minister of Finance was no doubt thinking of earlier occasions when the Minister of the day did seem to shirk his responsibility. Even as far back as 1941 the Minister of Finance of that day, a very highly regarded Minister indeed, Mr. Ilsley, asserted at pages 3376 and 3377 of Hansard, when answering a question in the House extemporaneously, that the Government had no control over the policies of the Central Bank, although Mr. Ilsley did reverse his stand a few days later by saying:
The point which I would like to emphasize is that the responsibility with which the Governor and Board have been charged by Parliament does not in any way relieve the Government of responsibility for the monetary policy being pursued by the Bank, nor in any way militate against public control of monetary policy.
That is to be found at page 3936 of Hansard for 1941. Mr. Abbott, the next Minister of Finance, concluded some remarks on the relations between the Bank and the Government by saying in 1951, as reported at page 4393 of Hansard:
The Government, of course, if it were not satisfied with the action taken by the Governor and the directors of the Bank of Canada, would have to change the management of the Bank.
And a little later on Mr. Abbott said:
So that I suppose it is fair to assume that the ultimate responsibility must fall upon the Government.
That is not exactly the strongest statement, certainly not as strong as was stated by the Minister of Finance last night. However, I think one can say that neither Mr. Ilsley nor Mr. Abbott shirked their respon-

sibility. By 1956, however, the Minister of Finance at that time, Mr. Harris, began to disclaim any responsibility for the restrictive actions of the Bank of Canada. On August 10 of that year, in reply to a question concerning the rise in bank rate announced by the Bank of Canada the preceding day, Mr. Harris said, as reported at page 7351 of Hansard, that the regulation of bank rate is a "duty and responsibility . . . imposed upon the bank and not upon the government". He also drew attention to the fact that a few months before he had asserted the principle that the actions of the bank are taken on the sole responsibility of the Governor. Then Mr. Harris went on to say, as reported at page 7352, that the proper interpretation of the Bank of Canada Act was that it was designed "to vest in the officials of the bank independent authority".
Mr. Fleming, then in opposition, took great umbrage to this, stating a day or so later that:
The government cannot shed Its responsibility for full fiscal policy in the broadest sense of the word, and that must include the actions of the Bank of Canada, even when, in a technical sense, those actions are taken by the Governor of the Bank of Canada in the exercise of the powers conferred upon him by the Bank of Canada Act.
But Mr. Fleming's view greatly altered only three years later-it was absolutely transformed-when he became Minister of Finance in the Diefenbaker Government. In 1959 it was he who asserted, at page 3098 of Hansard, that the Bank, not the Government, was responsible for monetary policy. He said:
-the government, as such, does not exercise control over the money supply or over the amount in circulation.
Then a little later he added:
The Government does not exert any sway in the field of monetary policy.
He, I would say, went farthest of all in denying the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. All this, I would like to remind hon. Members, is really a far cry from the remarks of Mr. Dunning, the Minister of Finance at the time of the debate over the nationalization of the Bank of Canada, although we sometimes think that this evasion of responsibility was something that had been very prominent at the time the Bank was created, and particularly at the time it was nationalized. Mr. Dunning, however, said in 1936, at page 3260 of Hansard, in the debate on the nationalization of the Bank:
The matter of public ownership is in my opinion much less important than that of Government
May 14, 1965

control. If we study the constitution of central banks from this aspect, we shall find ample precedent for the attempt which we are making to give the Government adequate control over the Bank of Canada.
I would argue, therefore, that what we are doing, or attempting to do, in this new section 14 is really to restore the kind of philosophy that was expressed by the Minister of Finance at that time, Mr. Dunning, and adhered to, to a substantial extent, by Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Abbott. We are trying to get to a situation where there will not be such a close relationship between the expressed connection of the Government of the day with the Bank on the one hand and the Bank's popularity rating on the other; because what really has happened, of course, is that since about mid-1955, since the Bank began to pursue a so-called tight money policy, the Government has been seeing that accepting full responsibility for monetary policy might incur political costs.
This, I take it, will no longer be possible. Now, under the new section 14, if someone in opposition asks the Minister his position in relation to bank policy, he will say either he agrees or he does not agree, if he is pressed to do so. If he does not agree, he will not be able to shirk responsibility any longer. He will, in the ultimate case, issue a directive as provided in subsection (2), with which the bank shall comply. Therefore I commend the Government for introducing this amendment which will prevent any further denial of ultimate responsibility on the part of the Minister of the day.
There are, however, one or two things that bother me a little about this proposed set-up, and I would be grateful to know a bit more about these problems. It seems to me that this sort of two-point set-up takes care only of the ideal situation on the one hand and of the extremely bad one on the other, and not really very much in between.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In the ideal situation the first part of the newly-defined relationship would operate; that is to say, there would be regular and harmonious consultation between the Minister or Deputy Minister of Finance on the one hand, and the Governor and other officials of the Bank of Canada on the other hand-the situation we have had during the past two or three years. In the extremely bad situation, when the first element of consultation has broken down entirely, the second part of the newly defined relationship would operate; that is to say, a directive would be issued,
Bank of Canada Act
and if the Governor of the bank did not like it he would resign.
At least, I assume that that is what would take place, although I am not at all sure that if this directive power had been in the Act at the time of the Coyne crisis it could in fact have been used, because it seems to me that the disagreement then was not really on monetary policy. Certainly it was not confined to monetary policy. As a matter of fact, the fiscal policy of the Government was almost as restrictive as the monetary policy of the bank. For example, tax rates were still anti-inflationary and opinion on foreign exchange rates of the Department of Finance and the bank was practically identical. It seems to me that the disagreement between Mr. Coyne and the Government was not really on monetary policy primarily, but rather on the views of the Governor of that time on general economic policies; indeed, on political philosophy as well. Since the directive must be limited to "a written directive concerning monetary policy", I am not at all sure that it could have been used at that time.
However, in a way perhaps it is beside the point that I am making, which is that it seems to me only in the extremely bad, almost crisis situation would subsection (2) in fact take effect and a directive be issued. What I am a little worried about is what you might call the in-between situation, when you have fairly adequate consultation and a fair degree of harmony no doubt, but the Bank feels that certain policies should in fact be pursued about which the Minister and the Government are not entirely happy. In fact, the latter would like to see some variations of the policy, and there is a situation where, in the course of consultation and discussion, the two parties have not been able to reach agreement. But there is not a situation of crisis proportions. In such a situation as that one really cannot-at least I cannot-visualize the Minister issuing a directive saying, for example, to take one instance, that the money supply should be increased by (j per cent in the following six months. For one thing I think the Government would be reluctant to do this publicly- and of course this has to be public, as subsection (3) points out-because it would appear to be an acknowledgement of the existence of a crisis.
For another thing, I would be doubtful if the Governor of the Bank of Canada would, so to speak, take this lying down. I think it would constitute a rebuff. This type of direc-

May 14, 1965
Bank of Canada Act
tive would, I think, constitute a rebuff of his judgment. In effect, he would have been publicly told off. I think there would be the possibility that this would be difficult for him to take if a directive were used in this kind of in-between situation, of the type I have just suggested.
I think the only directive which might be used, which from the point of view both of the Government and of the Governor would really be acceptable to them both, would be in general terms. For example, it would direct that the Bank follow a policy of monetary expansion. But as I read subsection (2), such a directive is not possible because a directive has to be "in specific terms and applicable for a specified period". Nor do I think such a general directive would be very effective anyway. So it seems to me that, in fact, under this new clause a directive would probably never be used. Indeed it has never been used in those countries which have had it in their banking acts for years. And we would still be faced, to some extent at any rate, with this kind of in-between situation when in fact it might be, not as difficult as now, but somewhat difficult for a Minister of Finance to take responsibility for a particular policy he did not like.
I wonder too, whether his position in this House might not be a little difficult if someone said to him: "Well, do you in fact agree with what the Bank is doing? If you don't, why don't you issue a directive?" I do not want to raise all kinds of false alarms, but this sort of thing might happen. Although the new section will certainly prevent any blatant shirking of responsibility, such as we had with Mr. Fleming for example, it will not necessarily provide-
Is this gospel truth or your opinion?

Therefore I would hope that at some time we in this country will be able to come to a position where will agree that the Minister of Finance should be on top of the situation in a more positive way, where he does not have to wait to issue a directive, which I think is pretty unlikely ever to happen. As I was saying, the amendments to the National Housing Act in June last were tailored to meet every possible measure of provincial participation. The fact that Quebec has indicated through press reports of Mr. Laporte's recent statement that it intends to make a determined attack on the problems of lower income housing and on urban renewal leaves with me feelings of great satisfaction and anticipation. If it is possible to go ahead in Quebec along the lines indicated by the Ontario Housing Act, or some modified version of that Act, we can make great progress. Ontario has set up a housing corporation capable of moving quickly in any part of the province, city, town or village. A survey is made, and if help is needed from C.M.H.C. to make the survey, such help is provided. If a request is made for a loan, C.M.H.C. provides 90 per cent of the money and the provincial corporation puts up the initial 10 per cent payment needed. Similar action is possible in Quebec, so I am hopeful that as a result of our meeting in Quebec City there will be renewed activity in this field so that we shall be able to do much more with respect to housing in the Province of Quebec.
The hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi was concerned about the need for greater home ownership in the Province of Quebec. He was interested in rural housing as much as in houses in urban communities. I assure the Committee there is nothing in the National Housing Act which says that rural housing shall be excluded from the benefit of its provisions. The same avenues are open to rural as to urban communities.
It might be worth while to draw the attention of the committee to two interesting and successful housing experiments carried on in the Maritime Provinces in Nova Scotia andl Prince Edward Island. They have set up cooperative organizations there to deal with the housing problem in rural areas, in small communities, so that senior citizens and handicapped people will be able to live in homes in or close to the communities where they have lived for most of their lives. The hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi asked for figures showing what has actually been done since the passing of the amendments to the Act last June in the field of urban renewal. The Committee might be interested to know that when this legislation was passed there had been approximately 44 urban renewal studies made in Canada. We have now reached the stage where nearly 60 studies have been made and requests have come in for 16 additional studies. This is largely as a result of the passing of the amendments and the publicity attending it, including the educational program through the symposia which have been held since that time. Ten urban renewal studies have been approved since June last under part V of the Act. In addition to these studies assistance has been approved for the preparation of 10 urban renewal schemes under section 23A and a further two applications for such assistance are under consideration at the present time. Since last June assistance has been approved for the implementation of 4 urban renewal schemes under section 23B of the Act. The total cost of these urban renewal projects is estimated at $15.6 million of which the Federal Government's share would amount to approximately $8 million.
Under the new legislation, assistance had been approved for the construction of 14 public housing projects comprising approximately 607 units under section 35D. The total Federal Government loans on these projects amounts to a little less than $8 million. Furthermore, an additional 2,920 public housing units to be constructed under section 35D have been approved for investigation in 18 municipalities and an additional 2,743 units are also currently being considered in 16 other municipalities.
